units.title: Matter, Measurement & Lab Safety
units.anchoring_phenomenon: A sealed bag of microwave popcorn increases in size when heated but does not change in mass. What is happening to the matter inside?
essential_questions: How can we classify different types of matter based on their properties?
Why is precise measurement important in scientific investigation?
What safety protocols protect us during laboratory work?
units.crse_theme: Students explore how cultural practices around food preparation (e.g., nixtamalization of corn, fermentation in kimchi) involve chemical and physical changes, connecting indigenous and global knowledge systems to chemistry concepts.
investigations: Investigation 1: Classifying Unknown Substances by Physical Properties

lessons.title: Classifying Matter
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can classify matter as pure substances or mixtures based on observable and measurable properties.
lessons.circle_prompt: Share one thing you observed on your way to school today that involved a change in matter (ice melting, steam from a vent, food cooking, etc.).
lessons.do_now: Look at the four items on your desk (salt, sand, a penny, and trail mix). Sort them into two groups and be ready to explain your reasoning.

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Sample set per group: salt, sand, iron filings, trail mix, distilled water

engage.description: Show a short video clip of a street food vendor making cotton candy. Ask: Is cotton candy the same substance as the sugar that went in? Students turn-and-talk.

explore.description: In groups of 3, students examine the sample set using hand lenses and magnets. They record observations in a T-chart (what they see vs. what they infer about composition). Groups attempt to sort substances into categories.

explain.description: Teacher-led discussion building the classification hierarchy: Matter -> Pure Substances (Elements, Compounds) and Mixtures (Homogeneous, Heterogeneous). Students label their samples using the new vocabulary and update their graphic organizer.

elaborate.description: Students receive three new mystery samples and must classify them using the framework. They write a justification sentence for each using the Because/But/So structure.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Given a description of a substance, students identify it as element, compound, homogeneous mixture, or heterogeneous mixture and provide one piece of evidence.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-filled graphic organizer with key terms and definitions; pair with a peer mentor during the Explore phase.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the classification activity as designed with the graphic organizer scaffold.
differentiation.advanced: Challenge students to propose a method to separate each mixture and explain the physical principle behind each separation technique.
differentiation.ell: Provide a bilingual vocabulary list (Spanish/English); use visual cues on the classification chart; allow verbal responses during the Evaluate phase.
differentiation.iep: Extended time on exit ticket; preferential seating near the anchor chart; provide a word bank for written responses.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how indigenous peoples classified natural materials (plants, minerals, animal products) for medicine, construction, and art long before modern chemistry formalized these categories.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences: Students write three sentences about matter classification using each conjunction. Example stem: 'Trail mix is a heterogeneous mixture...'

vocabulary.definition: Anything that has mass and takes up space
Matter with a fixed composition that cannot be separated by physical means
A pure substance made of only one type of atom
A pure substance made of two or more elements chemically combined
Two or more substances physically combined that retain their properties
A mixture with uniform composition throughout
A mixture with visibly different parts or phases

guided_notes_outline: Section 2: Pure Substances — Elements vs. Compounds

cer.phenomenon: You are given three unknown white powders labeled A, B, and C. Powder A dissolves completely in water and the solution tastes salty. Powder B does not dissolve and feels gritty. Powder C dissolves in water but the solution tastes sweet. Using only physical properties, classify each powder.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the observed physical properties, I claim that Powder A is a..., Powder B is a..., and Powder C is a...
cer.evidence_source: Use data from your observations table (solubility, taste, texture) to identify at least two properties per substance that support your classification.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the physical properties of each powder are consistent with the characteristics of [category], which is defined as...

lessons.title: Measurement and Significant Figures
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can take accurate measurements using appropriate tools and express them with the correct number of significant figures.
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time when a measurement really mattered — cooking, building something, a game. What happened when the measurement was off?
lessons.do_now: Estimate the length of your desk in centimeters. Write your estimate, then measure with a ruler. How close were you?

dci: PS1.A: Structure and Properties of Matter

materials: Graduated cylinders (10 mL and 100 mL per group)

engage.description: Show the NASA Mars Climate Orbiter disaster story — a $125 million spacecraft lost because of a unit conversion error. Ask: Why do units and precision matter in science?

explore.description: Station rotation: Students measure the same set of objects at 4 stations (length, mass, liquid volume, irregular solid volume). They record all measurements with units.

explain.description: Introduce significant figures rules. Students revisit their measurements and determine the correct number of sig figs for each. Class discusses why different tools give different levels of precision.

elaborate.description: Practice problems: Students calculate density using their measurements and express answers with the correct number of significant figures.

evaluate.description: Quick-write: Explain in 2-3 sentences why significant figures matter in scientific measurements. Use at least one specific example from today's lab.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a measurement checklist for each station; include unit conversion reference card.
differentiation.on_level: Complete station rotation and sig fig practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate percent error for each measurement and analyze which tools are most precise.
differentiation.ell: Label all measurement tools in English and native language; provide sentence frames for the quick-write.
differentiation.iep: Allow use of calculator for sig fig problems; provide extra time at stations; reduce number of practice problems.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how ancient civilizations developed precise measurement systems (Egyptian cubits, Chinese chi) and how measurement standards reflect cultural values and needs.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: Students write sentences embedding a definition as an appositive. Example: 'Significant figures, the meaningful digits in a measurement, tell us how precise our tools are.'

vocabulary.definition: The digits in a measurement that are known with certainty plus one estimated digit
How close repeated measurements are to each other
How close a measurement is to the true or accepted value
The curved surface of a liquid in a graduated cylinder

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Why Measurement Matters in Science
Section 2: SI Units and Common Conversions
Section 3: Rules for Counting Significant Figures
